“Dreaming: psychoanalysis or neurobiology?” (May 5, 2012) was the third in the “Minding the Gap” series of conferences sponsored by the New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (NYPSI). As initiator and principal organizer of the series, I would like to thank NYPSI for its support of the first three conferences and also extend a special thank you to Mt. Sinai Medical Center and the Pfeffer Center for Neuropsychoanalysis for their assistance in sponsoring this particular meeting, the final event in the year-long celebration of the centenary of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute.

The “Minding the Gap” series is devoted to bringing those of opposing viewpoints on psychoanalysis together in dialogue. The first such conference addressed Relational versus classical perspectives; the second focused on the etiology and treatment of psychosis, that is, the medical versus the psychosocial models of severe mental disorders. The dream conference emanated from the dream theory debate begun some years ago by Allan Hobson and Mark Solms. I will leave it to Drs. Hobson and Solms—and to the eminent dream theorists whose responses to their papers and aspects of their own distinctive research and thinking on dreaming appear here—to argue for and against the primary issues. Suffice it to say by way of introduction that Freud's dream theory was at the center of the controversy from the start. The notion that dreams are “the fulfilment of a wish,” the disguised fulfillment of a wish,” the “disguised fulfilment of a repressed wish,” and the “disguised fulfilment of a repressed, infantile wish” (Freud Museum London, n.d.) was refuted by Allan Hobson some 35 years ago.

The fictitious case of a professor having a midlife crisis is used to illustrate several points: 1) that our understanding of patients' dreams expands as more information becomes available; 2) subsequent interpretations don't invalidate earlier ones; 3) consciousness in psychoanalysis means something different than it does in neurology, knowledge and self-awareness being very different things; 4) significant actions cannot be assigned to either the ego or the id, but always to both; 5) concepts such as Ego and Id are ways of organizing aspects of thought and behavior; 6) the tendency to reify so-called psychic agencies and to locate them in specific areas of the brain seems questionable; and 7) the phrasing of interpretations expresses the emotional reactions of analysts to their patients' behavior.

Modern sleep and dream science not only fails to support the central tenets of Freudian dream theory but raises serious questions about other strongly held psychodynamic assumptions including the nature of the unconscious mind, infantile sexuality, the tripartite model of the mind, the concept of ego defense, free association and the analysis of the transference as a way of effecting adaptive change. This article summarizes a radical revision of psychodynamic theory in terms of the neurobiological findings of the last half century and proposes an alternative theoretical model which posits a virtual reality generator for the brain that arises late in evolution and early in the development of thermoregulating animals. The author's training and clinical experience are used to highlight these theoretical considerations and inform a forthcoming treatment-oriented book in progress entitled EGO DAMAGE AND REPAIR.

The subtitle of Wearing My Tutu to Analysis is Learning Psychodynamic Concepts from Life, and, in an artful and compelling way, the authors afford just such an opportunity to the reader. Each chapter begins with a clinical or illustrative personal story, followed by a section of the authors' psychoanalytic reflections on the story. Each reflection

128

discusses the previous story in light of pertinent psychoanalytic concepts. The uninitiated reader will learn a good deal about psychoanalysis through the application of psychoanalytic theory in revealing the layers of meaning in the stories.

Psychoanalytic concepts covered in Wearing My Tutu to Analysis include a broad range: from mentalization to psychic equivalence; object; transitional object; the depressive position; sadomasochism; transference and countertransference; analytic abstinence; boundary violations; the frame; the Oedipal complex; idealized love; and dissociation. The range of theorists the reader is introduced to, albeit briefly, is amazing: from Freud, Ferenczi, Klein and Fenichel to Bergman; Winnicott; Kohut; Stolorow and Atwood; Deutsch; Benedek; Mahler; Pine; Jacobson, Phillips, Poland, Harold Blum, Meissner; Bach; Mitchell; Bucci; Yalom; Beebe and Lachman; Sullivan; Fonagy, Fairbairn, Bowlby, and Victor Frankl.

The stories the authors tell are immediate, affectively alive, and experience-near. The reader is repeatedly drawn into them. The reflections are accessible yet sophisticated applications of psychoanalytic concepts. It is striking that although there were three authors contributing to these reflections they are told in as seamless and consistent a voice as if they had been written by one person.

This book would make a strong introductory text for college courses in psychoanalysis as well as for the general reader interested in psychoanalysis. To this point, the authors state, “Poland's idea of ‘interpretive attitude’ within which the patient can ‘listen in’ on his internal processes in the presence of an attentive therapist can be understood as the core of therapeutic action … [allowing] the patient gradually to internalize a similar attitude of curiosity and openness toward his own inner world” (p. 132). The reader of Wearing My Tutu is afforded a similar opportunity to that which the patient gets from “listening in” on the analyst's interpretations.

As is well known, Freud frequently missed the boat in his efforts to explicate female psychology. For several decades, brave, thoughtful, and mostly female analysts have been revising his misconceptions and blind spots. These women are smart, articulate, and sometimes even respectful of the early psychoanalytic efforts to understand feminine developmental pathways. Among these revisionists, no voice is more vibrant and intelligent than that of Rosemary Balsam. In the company of other creative observers, Balsam explores and maps the vastly variegated terrain of female development. This important book brings together updated versions of many of her articles and book chapters written from 1996 to the present on the subject.

Balsam is a training and supervising analyst at the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis as well as the current coeditor of the book review section of the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association. As such, she possesses many years of clinical experience as well as a wide-ranging knowledge of traditional and contemporary psychoanalytic literature. Although she acknowledges the “contemporary ego psychological slant” to her thinking, she is mindful and appreciative of the advances made by those outside that perspective. She can, however, be critical of the direction taken by those thinkers who emphasize internalized object relations at the expense of attending to the impact of flesh and blood bodies both our own and our patients'. As Chodorow and Harris remind us in their foreword to the book, “there is always a physically and psychically embodied patient in relation to a physically and psychically embodied analyst, not only a mind in relation to another mind” (p. xii) meeting in the consulting room.

The central thesis of Women's Bodies in Psychoanalysis is the neglect of the female body in all its physicality and procreative power in most psychoanalytic writing and theorizing past and present. Balsam pays homage to Freud and his observation that the ego was first and foremost a body ego.

With psychoanalysis now more securely ensconced in university humanities departments rather than in their traditional clinical settings, it becomes a matter of some importance to ask how these disparate realms will engage in dialogue that can enhance our therapeutic sensibilities. The essays in Unconscious Dominions exemplify this split, highlighting our difficulty in approaching these Ivory Tower intellectual debates and establishing their relevance to practice, while also warning us that we ignore these debates at our peril. This edited volume can seem at times overloaded with senseless claims and unfortunate jargon that could allow for its easy dismissal, but for those who persevere beyond the obscure, there is a treasure trove of historical developments and theoretical questions about the incorporation of psychoanalytic ideas and practice into colonial spaces during the late 19th and 20th centuries, when European imperialism was at its height. The book explores how psychoanalysis, both as a clinical practice and a discourse, champions a particular type of person who comes to knows him- or herself in a particular type of way: a self organized around questions of desire (id), self-reflection (ego), and morality laced with judgment (superego). But how could such a discourse meet and be used to understand those whose self-experience lays outside this version of subjectivity born within the height of European modernity? Indeed, could—and can—such a distinctive style of imagining, or governing, the self, its past, and its (hidden) motivations travel to make sense of an Other? In asking these questions, the editors highlight how the Freudian subject, evocative as it is, was also a model of subjectivity permeated with 19th-century modernity and morality. For Freud, man's neurosis results from forcing instinctual drives to live in a social world structured by demands that thwart them. Civilization is made possible through the ego and superego, but in its undertow, argues the editors, lies a perpetual shadow of a primitive Other; the uncivilized who answers not to his ego but to his passions.

This article, by a nonclinican, raises in a largely personal way questions about class and the pursuit of justice from a psychoanalytic perspective. It considers some of the channels that may have been opened—regardless of intent, or ideological leaning—by the interpersonal and relational schools and, more specifically, by Philip Bromberg's work on shame, dissociation, and self-states. The point here is not to fault Bromberg's psychoanalytic work for being insufficiently directed at social justice movements, but, rather, to make clear that the political project of psychoanalysis generally may find its more just future partly through unexpected channels of clinical thought and clinical practice.

This article makes a brief contribution to the ongoing dialogue on dreams between neuroscience and psychoanalysis by linking several converging lines of evidence. Recent evidence indicates that the default mode network (DMN), a highly interconnected set of “hubs” in the brain, is active during sleep. In addition, activity in the DMN is strongly associated with mental imagery that is not directly tied to current perception (“stimulus-independent thought”), which is also a central feature of dreams. Finally, the elimination of dreams is correlated with lesions in areas that have a high degree of overlap with two regions of the DMN, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and the temporo-occipital junction. Given that the vmPFC is a key node in brain circuitry regulating motivation, these converging lines of evidence support the basic psychoanalytic idea that dreams arise from wishful impulses and other emotional motivations.

Ethics is a topic that has held little interest for me. Like Nietzsche, I tend to see it as a way of controlling people's minds. Not that it lacks importance, but usually the conversation is captured and directed by those seeking moral safety or conformity. Newspaper columns on

649

ethical behavior that answer reader's queries about the correct thing to do strike me as little more than Emily Post for the worried and the guilt-ridden.

So it came as a great relief to find that David Levine would agree. This book is not about ethical conduct, doing the right thing, or being good. As the title says, it is about the “capacity” for ethical conduct. What does it take to think in an ethical way, to be capable of ethical behavior? Levine's answer has to do essentially with being authentic, emotionally alive, and reflective. As a result, he does not get bogged down in the age-old conflict between the head and the heart, our impulses and our judgment, or our desires and our duty. He gives us a chance to think about it in a new way.

And new thinking is desperately needed. We may be obsessed with the desire to be “ethical” or correct in our personal conduct, but we live in an ethically challenged age. Almost daily we read about corruption in government, as elected officials are exposed in the act of promoting their personal economic interests or covering up their sordid private lives. The legislative process is driven by influence peddling, while a “revolving door” separates regulators from lobbyists. Super PACs drive our electoral system, giving big donors “access” to politicians. Insider trading is rampant in financial markets, financial ratings firms bid for business from the very clients they rate, and personal information is regularly leaked or sold. We read about how consumer product reliability and quality are routinely compromised by the drive for profit.

Levine does not directly address the rise of money in our society, but it clearly forms the backdrop of his thinking. We are in a phase of “investor capitalism,” driven by the financial industry, in which the demand to increase a company's stock prices, known now as “shareholder value,” trumps all other considerations for management. This inevitably leads to conflict between the inherent value of products and services and how those values are ranked in financial markets. Although Levine steers clear of such larger economic and social analysis, he is acutely aware of the tensions in organization between actually functioning effectively to produce the goods and services that define their business and the pressures that subvert those goals and lead to “creative” accounting methods, procedures that disguise costs and inflate profits, “informal” forms of reporting, as well as fraud, espionage, and corruption. This, of course, leads to splitting and fragmentation as the contradictions play out. He notes that “any pursuit of emotional ends other than those stemming from doing the job well has the potential to corrupt the work process” (p. 75).

As both a practicing psychoanalyst as well as an academically trained philosopher, Jon Mills offers a unique perspective on the current state of contemporary psychoanalysis. In Conundrums: A Critique of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Mills's analysis takes two distinct forms. In his opening chapters, Mills directly challenges many of the implicit philosophical underpinnings of Relational psychoanalysis. Subsequent chapters principally deal with the political and personal issues he has experienced when presenting these critiques in professional settings. These two styles of analysis are very different and necessitate a caveat before moving forward. Because I lack personal experience and direct knowledge of the delicate incidents he describes, especially in chapters 4-6, I choose to not engage with them. Instead, my goals in this review are to faithfully present the complex critiques of Relational psychoanalysis and then offer my thoughts on them in the discussion section.

In my role as a discussant of Galit Atlas's clinical material, I will first make some general remarks about what I believe the fundamental functions of dreaming are and how best to work with dreams, and then address Dr. Atlas's patient's dreams within their personal and psychoanalytic contexts.

Dreaming is thinking when we are asleep. By definition, dreaming is unconscious thinking, and I see it as the continuation of implicit and explicit processing that occurs during waking. It offers the best window into unconscious thinking.

And what do we dream about? We dream about our most immediate concerns: our dreams include attempts to resolve conflict, to self-regulate, to regulate affect, to envision and move developmentally, to fortress threatened patterns of organization, to consolidate new experience, and to integrate and enhance new learning. Daily events engage the deeper crosscurrents of our lives, activating organizing patterns that constrict or expand, vitalize or devitalize. In what I call the organizing model of dreaming, I have posited that the supraordinate functions of dreaming are to develop, maintain, and restore psychological organization and affect regulation in keeping with shifting motivational priorities (Fosshage, 1983, 1988, 1997, 2007, 2008). Although on one occasion, the dreamer will repeat a familiar, devitalizing way of being in relationship to others (activated during the previous day), on another occasion, the dreamer dreams of a new, expansive way of being, a new vitalizing experience of one's self.

This article proposes a defense termed narrative-identification, an obsessive focus on generic narratives as stand-ins for historical human objects. The article provides a clinical illustration in which a female trauma survivor's masochistic obsession with predator-prey news stories insulated her from emotional spontaneity in her personal relationships, and concealed a core transference element in her work with me—that is, her fear of my becoming a sadistic aggressor. Rather than interacting with me, the patient interacted with her news stories, as if they were dominating, sadistic objects in their own right (termed here narrative-objects). It is asserted that the patient's identification with such deindividualized, abstract states as stand-ins for human objects mitigated a sense of assault from her sadistic historical objects and facilitated her avoidance of engaging with projective-introjective processes in the transference. This type of identification with abstract states is categorized as nonpenetrating (identifications that do not stimulate introjection of aspects of the other) and is based on the following assumption: the less individualized the object of identification, the more schizoid the psychological functioning of the subject. A turning point in the treatment occurred when the patient expressed her fear of my spoken thoughts, which might suddenly and without warning introduce new topics from which she would feel compelled to create sadistic narrative-objects. This made clear my underlying transference role as a passively sadistic object, the patient's historical mother. Such a realization began the transformation of the patient's generic narrative-objects into an enlivened personal narrative that housed a central historical object—her sadistic mother with whom I was linked in the transference.

This article brings us into the heart of a long-term analytic treatment relationship in order to illustrate, perhaps extend, Phillip Bromberg's creative thinking about the functions of multiplicity, dissociation, and integration in human self structure. We follow how my patient Tanya's capacity for access to her multiplicity played a key role in deepening the negotiation of our relationship as well as in resisting the environmental pull towards over-accommodating, dissociative integrations—identity foreclosures (Erikson, 1980)—in her own development.

More broadly, the article suggests that the centrality of a dialectical tension (including mind-body tension) between a unified experience of self-sameness and an experience of one's multiplicity goes well beyond its functions in managing individual trauma. It may represent a crucial evolved human adaptation to the existential challenge of creating and recreating meaning in face of the ambiguity, hidden multiplicity, deceptiveness, and bias inherent in even the good-enough relational world.

Patients like Tanya thus require not only that we empathize deeply with their experience, but that we allow them to open the often hidden multiplicity in ourselves. In so doing, we will confront the tensions between multiplicity and integration that are a fundamental dimension of human experience as well as the shared, existential truths carried within each patient's trauma. Bromberg's vision, including his attunement to surprise, irony, and paradox, can encourage the radical theoretical openness—indeed theoretical multiplicity—needed to facilitate this challenging, highly personal, reciprocal process.

This article discusses present-day culturally facilitated fetishizations of the body and how these may account for a variety of sexual disorders in women. It is proposed that a hallmark of female perverse relating is self-objectification in an effort to control a dangerous subjectivity within. This is in contrast to typical male perverse relating, which largely revolves around objectifying others as a means to control the dangerous subjectivity of the other. The danger that is often feared by women is localized within as an intense, uncontrollable (and feared excessive) desire, concretized as a voracious appetite. In some cases, this fear may culminate in an obsession with remaining thin, reflecting a wish to control a self-experience of wanting too much, desiring too much, or becoming or being too big. A self-structure, the Objectified Self, is offered as a way to visualize the dissociated, relatively nonaffective position of constructed self-experience in relation to these fears and is schematized as derived from the Subjective Object or the self for others. An unconscious fear of “phallic” power is proposed as an unconscious conviction in many women who struggle with assertion, thrust, and the dread of being too big, too potent, or too strong.

This issue of contemporary psychoanalysis is a celebration of Object Relations in Psychoanalytic Theory (1983). In the 30 years since Jay Greenberg and Stephen Mitchell published their now classic examination of comparative psychoanalytic theories, we can fully appreciate just how seminal and groundbreaking this volume was to be.

The idea for a special issue grew out of a panel held at the William Alanson White Institute in September 2010, which was organized by Pasquale Pantone, Director of Clinical Education, to pay tribute to the book. What follows is Dr. Pantone's description of the birth of that meeting and the subsequent remarks of the panelists. Together, these papers offer a unique perspective on an essential aspect of the Interpersonal/Relational turn in psychoanalysis and the guiding role that psychoanalysts at the White Institute have played in that development.

We have also invited a range of psychoanalytic writers to share their view of the book's impact on, and place in, the history of analytic ideas. Each author, of course, writes from a unique vantage point influenced by his or her theoretical position. We begin with Dr. Jack Drescher's 1993-1994 interviews of Jay Greenberg and Steve Mitchell. These memorable accounts, first published in The White Society Voice, capture the authors' intellectual vigor and exuberant idealism as they assumed key editorial roles in the years after the successful launching of their book. We follow with Robert Michels's paper, an eloquent defense of the drive model against theoretical pluralism. He praises Greenberg and Mitchell's attempt to establish a comparative psychoanalysis, yet takes issue with their methodology and argues theoretical merit should be tested by clinical results rather than philosophical premise or historical context.

The interchange of ideas between neurobiology and psychoanalysis needs to include the latest ideas of both fields. Psychoanalysis has greatly revised its theory of dream formation and the clinical approach to working with dreams, including the role of disguise in dream formation and the need for associations in dream understanding. Both the Freudian and the activation-synthesis models of dream formation are two-stage; neither two-stage model may best account for the data. Whereas Jung describes dreaming as an analogue to schizophrenia, and Hobson considers it an analogue to delirium, we need to also attend to the ways that mental functioning during dreaming may be superior to waking functioning.

Dreams, food, associations, metaphor, cooking, cocreation, pregnancy

This short case presentation focuses on dreams as a way to open a symbolic play space. Sophie comes to therapy and asks for what we later name “fast food” in order to help her grow, have a healthy intimate relationship, and get married. She begins her work in a state of agitation, very concrete, desperately asking again and again: “What should I do? Is anything going to change soon?” Our main focus is on her desperation, hunger, and requests that I feed her as an omnipotent mother who knows everything about the past, present, and future. There is limited ability to know her mind, use symbolic language, or play with the “food” I offer; rather it is as if Sophie has to immediately “swallow” anything I give her. In the room, the use of food becomes our first playful metaphor. I present four dreams from different points in Sophie's therapy, emphasizing the use of dreams not only to move from concrete to playful and symbolic thinking, but also to enhance her ownership of her own mind and subjectivity to a point when she can “have her own kitchen, cook her own food,” and even feed her analyst.

Sleep in the countertransference, a not uncommon phenomenon, is rarely spoken of because of the shame associated with it and the difficulty registering, remembering, and finding words for unconscious elements that set the stage for and trigger its occurrence. The article begins, as did the clinical experiences it seeks to formulate, with a dramatic instance of what felt like sudden death. The author describes several examples of this phenomenon and how he has learned to understand and work with it clinically. It occurs in the context of empathic immersion in—and disconnection from—the patient's nonverbal emotional core. It may be sudden and massive, or subtle and gradual—with clouding of consciousness over which the analyst has no control once it goes beyond a certain “event horizon” analogous to that described around black holes in outer space. There are many psychoanalytic, poetic, and religious ways of wording what the author considers a regressive “phase in the motions and transformations of psychic life” (Loewald, 1981). In some cases, it may even be crucial to the reanimation of buried or dissociated aspects of both patient and analyst.

This is a personal response to the interview of Philip Bromberg in this journal in which I discuss my intellectual resonance with his thinking as well as some important conceptual differences. In order to elaborate some of the invaluable aspects of his thought, as well as questions that arise from it, I refer to Philip's other writings. Although I base my agreement on ideas about affect regulation, attachment, dissociation, and intersubjectivity, the focus of my discussion is the difference between thinking in terms of a movement from dissociation to conflict versus a movement from dissociation to recognition. I suggest that some of the issues Philip describes as the problem of accepting the “giftie” of being shown how we appear to the other and the “imposition of meaning” can be further elaborated in terms of my distinction between complementarity and thirdness. I discuss one of the cases in the recent book, Shadow of the Tsunami, in order to illustrate how the analyst's dissociation relates specifically to difficulties acknowledging conflict between “good” and “bad,” loving and hateful aspects of both self and other.

paternal function, father, masculinity, triangulation, thirdness, pre-Oedipal development

In the context of changing constructions of gender and family structure, this article addresses two related aims. First, it aims to develop a focused and comprehensive understanding of what is termed the “paternal function” as understood within object relations theory. Second, it offers a critique of existing theory, arguing that the literature reflects some conflation between function and functionary, or between maleness and/or masculinity and the performance of this function or set of functions. Although the term “paternal function” is frequently employed in the psychoanalytic literature, a common understanding of what it constitutes cannot be assumed. The construct appears to encompass several different dimensions, four of which are explored in the article. The authors contend that paternal function should be understood as distinct from the role of the father in the life of the infant. This opens a space to consider alternative sources of parental functioning and the related importance of the position of third persons or objects in infant development. It is argued that critical engagement with the construct of the paternal function not only has relevance for rethinking developmental theory and childrearing practices, but that it may also prove potentially valuable to case formulations and understanding interactional dynamics within the therapeutic relationship.

I offer a retrospective view of the evolving baby metaphor in relational thinking. Early relational critiques of developmental tilt models and the concept of holding in clinical work, amplified by feminist writers, sharply skewed relationalists toward a vision of the patient-as-adult and a view of the analytic dialogue as inherently intersubjective. Bringing my own Winnicottian/relational perspective to this critique, I expanded the notion of holding and proposed a way to bridge Winnicottian holding with a relational perspective by exploring the analyst's participation in establishing and maintaining a holding experience. Here, I review and update this controversy, offering new ideas about holding's clinical function in buffering shame states.

An Interview with Philip M. Bromberg Ph.D.

Don Greif PHD and Ruth Livingston PHD

Ruth Livingston

Ruth Livingston  

Editors' Note: Shortly after we began our editorship, Donnel Stern suggested that we devote a Special Issue to Philip Bromberg. We loved this idea, and got the ball rolling, requesting an interview with Philip and inviting a number of contributors to reflect on his body of work. There is no question that Philip's contributions to psychoanalysis over the past several decades are enormous—indeed, immeasurable. By elucidating the role of developmental trauma in shame-laden dissociative processes that impair relatedness, and by providing us with a language (e.g., multiple self-states) to comprehend this phenomenon, he has not only significantly expanded the scope of our theoretical understanding, but given us a way to see patients through fresh eyes and to connect empathically with them.

We met with Philip, our former teacher/supervisor, now friend and colleague, for more than two hours one wintry day. Philip requested that we send him a list of questions prior to our sit-down, and we did. Making our task much easier, he had prepared answers to these questions. During our time with him, we asked additional questions. The result is a rich and interactive exploration of Philip's clinical and theoretical thinking, as well as many personal reflections. Sitting with Philip was a treat; in the end, we knew that we had captured an extraordinary snapshot of what it is like to be a patient or student of Philip's, and how it feels to interact with him in his consulting room. We are very grateful.

In the interview that follows, questions in italics are the “formal” questions that we posed before our interview. You will see that his answers took us in many interesting directions. We hope, in reading this, you will feel as enriched as we did in his presence.

Don Greif, Ph.D.

Ruth H. Livingston, Ph.D.

attractors, character, complex systems, dissociation, hysteresis, self-organization, self-states

Philip Bromberg's seminal and highly influential theory of self-states will be addressed from the perspective of complex systems theory. In his writing about self-states, Bromberg makes explicit links to several of the ideas and concepts arising from the complex systems literature, including his discussion of the nonlinear and discontinuous nature of self-state transitions. In this article, I will draw parallels not directly taken up by Bromberg. First, I will discuss the fundamental dynamics and properties of Bromberg's theory of mind in terms of control and order parameters. Second, I will point out the relationship between Bromberg's self-states and configurations of self-states to the concepts of attractors and attractor landscapes. Third, I will use the concept of hysteresis to understand Bromberg's discussion of the proactive and protective function of “not-me” self-states.

What do geese dream of?” asks Freud (1900/1950a) in The Interpretation of Dreams. He answers “of maize.” “Pigs dream of acorns,” adds Ferenczi (1910) in a footnote. Contained within these succinct quotes, said to have originated in an Hungarian proverb, is the basic theory that dreams are wish fulfillments.

What does Sophie dream of? Surprisingly or not, in Sophie's dreams we can find many Freudian elements: aggression, war, sex, and, of course, food. She dreams of a dining hall, of a kitchen where people prepare her food, and, later on, where she can cook her own food. Her dreams refer to the War in Israel in 1973, to military commanders, missions in foreign countries, and include images of bags (vaginas?) and motorcycles (penises?). In her dreams, she loses stuff, is kidnapped, and she is hungry—very hungry.

As we know, there are as many psychoanalytic schools of thought as there are approaches to dreams. These approaches are strongly tied with the way one thinks about the analytic process itself. We can clearly see the link between analytic method and technique of dream analysis from Freud on. In the Freudian tradition, as Aron (1989) points out, dreams were used to prove the topographic model of the mind, the primary process functioning of the unconscious, the importance of infantile sexuality, and the usefulness of the free association method. Freud, who believed that the manifest dream is only a way to conceal and disguise the real contents and not to reveal the inner psychological life of the dreamer, minimized the organized quality of dreams, and considered that dreams were brought about exclusively through the primary process. Any aspect of dreams that reflected more organized thought was dismissed.

In 1972, the american psychoanalyst Harold Searles published an article in the Psychoanalytic Review titled “Unconscious Processes in Relation to the Environmental Crisis.” He cited a broad base of evidence for this crisis: the pollution of lakes, rivers, and oceans; the circulation of pesticides through the food chain; the leakage of radioactive waste; rapid overpopulation. “My hypothesis,” he wrote, “is that man is hampered in his meeting of this environmental crisis by a severe and pervasive apathy which is based largely upon feelings and attitudes of which he is unconscious.” Searles called on fellow analysts to “make some real contribution, along with our brothers in other fields of science, toward meeting the ecological crisis” (Searles, 1972, p. 361). Four decades later, they have begun to heed his call.

Engaging with Climate Change is the result of an interdisciplinary conference at the Institute of Psychoanalysis in London in 2010, organized by the British psychoanalyst Sally Weintrobe. The 22 authors have varied backgrounds: psychoanalysis, climate science, environmental policy and communications, sociology, economics, and environmental philosophy and ethics. The book's organization lends itself well to such a cross-disciplinary exchange, with most chapters followed by one or more commentaries from other authors. Because this format also leads to a fair amount of repetition, I will forego a chapter-by-chapter description and summarize the book's most important and original conclusions.

The book sets out from the premise that public inaction on global warming requires explanation. Commentators frequently note the “gap” that exists between scientific knowledge and public opinion, as well as between opinion and action. The problem can no longer be attributed to an “information deficit” or a lack of scientific consensus. Might it reflect instead unconscious psychological dynamics? In other words, what lessons might psychoanalysis hold for the current impasse on climate policy? And, conversely, what might psychoanalysts need to know about global warming in order to understand its implications for mental health?

“Unkind cutting back” is a “micro-traumatic” way of relating in which one person in a significant relationship withdraws—but only partially—from the other. The individual withdrawn from is made to feel insecure, deprived, and/or betrayed by the other's unilateral, unexpected retreat. The problem is compounded by there being a subtle proscription against naming and exploring the act's hurtful elements. A cutback's damage depends on the manner in which the attenuation occurs and the meaning assigned to it by each party. This article explores a variety of unkind cutbacks—whether psychological, concretely behavioral, or both—that may occur in everyday interactions and at various stages of life. It takes a close look at cutbacks in the frequency of sessions within the analytic relationship, a tricky move that is often instigated by one member and resisted by the other. The analytic challenge is to avoid being thrown off course by the narcissistic strains associated with the cutback bid, and to learn how to harness the ensuing exploration for maximal therapeutic advantage.

I am pleased and honored to contribute this introduction to an issue devoted to the work of Philip Bromberg. The reasons for my feelings are both professional and personal. The professional reasons are obvious: Philip is one of the most influential psychoanalysts of our era. My work and thinking have been influenced as much by Philip as by anyone I know. I will detail some of that influence later on. But the personal reasons that I am pleased to be writing this piece go even deeper. Philip is one of my closest friends. He's always had my back.

I've known Philip a long time. I arrived in New York City in the fall of 1976, to attend the William Alanson White Institute. The world was a different place then—in the larger sense, of course, but also on the level of our little psychoanalytic world. Psychologists at institutes of the American Psychoanalytic Association still had to sign pledges that they were “research candidates” who would not engage in clinical practice; Klein, Winnicott, and Fairbairn were new and hard to understand for most Americans; Bion and Lacan were not even on the map, at least not yet in New York; countertransference was a new and controversial topic in clinical process. I had entered psychoanalytic training without having really even known a psychoanalyst (I'd had psychoanalytically oriented supervisors, but none who was formally trained), so it wasn't only the ideas and practices of psychoanalysis that I didn't yet understand—I didn't understand the politics, either. But because I soon immersed myself in the psychoanalytic literature, I did notice within a fairly brief period of time that my teachers at White had little opportunity to publish anywhere but in Contemporary Psychoanalysis and one or two other nonmainstream outlets. I had to attend to the painful fact that these teachers of mine, whose work had begun to inspire me and in whom I was beginning to feel such pride, were not accepted as psychoanalysts by the analysts of certain other institutes in town.

Psychoanalysis and neurobiology are complementary approaches to the study of dreaming that have demonstrated significant convergences of findings. Hobson's tendentious effort to utilize neurobiology to disprove psychoanalysis is largely unsupported. The perspective of Barbara Jones, like Hobson a central contributor to neurobiology, illustrates an open and judicious approach. Solms has made a major contribution in demonstrating and elucidating the crucial role of the forebrain in dreaming. However, his model detaches dreaming from REM sleep and the brain stem to a degree that is unwarranted and limiting. A number of lines of evidence for a close relationship between dreaming and REM sleep, and for the relevance of the brain stem in dreaming, are delineated. Finally, many of the more specific and subtle aspects of the psychoanalytic theory of dreaming are seen as beyond the present reach of neurobiology. This is not a basis for discarding these elements, some of which have already found experimental and clinical support.

The most fundamental change in psychoanalytic thinking about dreams has to do with their place in mental life. Freud thought of dreams as mini-pathological events that occurred relatively rarely, about once or twice a night, when a wish arose that would disturb sleep. This viewpoint had to be revised when Aserinsky, Dement, and Kleitman discovered that we dream regularly throughout the night, at least every 90 minutes, and much more often than we consciously realize (Aserinsky & Kleitman, 1953; Dement & Kleitman, 1957a, 1957b). Today, we recognize that a dream is a mental event that occurs regularly throughout the night.

Because dreams are such a regular occurrence, it seems less sensible to look for a single cause of dreaming. If we keep asking “Why do we dream?” then also we shall have to ask, “Why do we think?” In neither case can we expect a single answer. Both thinking and dreaming are regularly occurring mental activities, both take many different forms, and both probably occur for many reasons.

There are many reasons that have been given for why we dream. I will summarize 10 of them:

to maintain sleep in the presence of unacceptable wishes (Freud, 1900/1950a);

to compensate for excessively one-sided conscious attitudes held during the day (Jung, 1948/1974);

if the dream is told, to communicate something to someone else that could not be said otherwise (Ferenczi, 1913/1980; Kanzer, 1955; Blechner, 1983);

The invitation to meet with you today in honor of the 1983 publication of this wonderful book evoked a wash of emotions and memories. I would like to start by talking a little about these earlier years and Stephen's involvement in the field of psychoanalysis.

Stephen chose to train at the White Institute, I think, in part because of the rich intellectual tradition and culture of innovative thinking he found here. He appreciated the importance of contextualizing psychoanalysis—of the need to understand it in interaction with its culture—for example, with political philosophy, feminism, and semiotics. I trained at the william alanson white institute from 1988 to 1992. I decided to go to White because, at the time, it was a first-rate institute where psychiatrists sought training and the only one that accepted openly gay candidates. The three New York psychoanalytic institutes affiliated with the American Psychoanalytic Association, where many of my teachers and supervisors were affiliated, would not open their programs' doors to openly gay candidates until 1991 (Drescher, 2002a).

I did not know at the time that being discriminated against would have a silver lining. In applying to White, I knew nothing about the language and theories of Interpersonal psychoanalysis or the evolving relational turn that would affect my future scholarly work. Instead, my dynamically oriented psychiatric training at Downstate Medical Center in Brooklyn (1981-1984) was steeped in traditional analytic orthodoxy, and our psychotherapy classes extolled the highly abstinent therapeutic framework of Robert Langs (1977). As residents, we were not exposed to the work of Sullivan or Fromm—a one-year course on Melanie Klein's work was considered daring enough. Finally, despite the fact that the American Psychiatric Association had removed homosexuality from the DSM in 1973 (Bayer, 1981; Drescher & Merlino, 2007), teachers still spoke of homosexuality in psychopathological terms. Needless to say, as residents we were not exposed to Steve Mitchell's already published critiques of what analysts at Downstate were teaching (Mitchell, 1978, 1981; Drescher, 2002b).

In 1983, Jay Greenberg and Stephen Mitchell published Object Relations in Psychoanalytic Theory. It brought Relational psychoanalysis, and the work of Sullivan and Object Relations analysts, more into the mainstream of Freudian psychoanalysis in North America. It was a significant effort to change the landscape of American psychoanalytic thinking and clinical work. This article looks at Greenberg and Mitchell's description of Melanie Klein's theories and her place in psychoanalytic thinking. The author suggests that Greenberg and Mitchell's focus on Klein and the drives limits our understanding of the far-reaching developments of Klein's clinical theory and method. The emphasis on Klein as another drive theorist who struggled with giving up the drives in favor of object relations, it is argued, minimizes the developments she fostered and lessens her significance as a major force in the world of psychoanalysis. The article describes the importance of Klein's clinical thinking and that of the Kleinians, its impact on the internal world and unconscious phantasy, and its clinical applications.

In his foreword to gohar homayounpour's engaging, lyrical book, film director Abbas Kiarostami writes, “[i]n the format of a biographical novel, and using psychoanalytic free association, she opens up windows and sheds light onto the darkness of the human soul” (p. xii). In a letter to his brother and sister, the poet John Keats wrote: “Call the world if you please ‘The vale of Soul-making’” (To George and Georgiana Keats, February 14, 1819, Keats, 1958, p. 102). Davies's timely book makes a similar point. Though we try our best to evade it, suffering, actively engaged, can become transformative. Davies goes beyond this to offer a critique of our culture's growing dread of emotional pain, and its strategies of avoidance and negation, implicating our profession in the project, to obscure and minimize the meaning that suffering can have.

I start with Keats, though, not just to suggest that Davies has important antecedents and allies but also to create an historical context for Davies's point. Beginning in the 18th and 19th centuries, the West was being forced to reconsider its attitude towards suffering. Before the Enlightenment, the conventional view, adumbrated in Keats's phrase, was that the world was a “vale of tears.” Suffering was inevitable, but, properly understood, provided opportunities to prepare for death and salvation. The Enlightenment undermined that belief, making suffering and all forms of deprivation, no longer the will of God, requiring that we endure it with faith, but a set of problems demanding alleviation if not solution.

Dreams, REM sleep, hallucination, wish fulfillment, theta rhythm, creativity

For decades Allan Hobson has proclaimed Freud's dream theory as thoroughly mistaken. He has also suggested that Freud's use of the mistaken tenets of 19th-century neurology undermined not just that theory, but also the fundamental psychoanalytic propositions of Freud's (1900/1950b) mental apparatus as conceptualized in Chapter 7 of The Interpretation of Dreams. He is wrong on both accounts! Freud's theory of dreams remains an accurate general framework in which to understand and explore the origins, nature, and meaning of dreams. In addition, embodied within Freud's model of the mental apparatus are inferences about brain processes not just relevant to dreams but also to conscious perception, memory, reality testing, and creativity that are remarkably consonant with modern neuroscientific understanding.

Anne Alvarez is one of our most distinguished clinicians and has earned an international reputation for her work with severely disturbed children. The Thinking Heart is the culmination of her work spanning more than five decades. This book will be of interest not only to child therapists but adult therapists as well. Despite the tremendous erudition that is on display, the book is written in a modest and personal voice as Alvarez shares her failures and her mistakes along with her successes. In this respect, her book is a gift of great personal generosity to our field. The sheer charm and modesty of it helps the reader to get comfortable and enjoy entering into what are progressively more intricate and sophisticated discussions.

Alvarez notes at the outset of The Thinking Heart that children coming into treatment today are more disturbed and damaged than they were half a century ago, which is to say that they are more cognitively delayed and emotionally impoverished than was observed previously. Alvarez acknowledges that although many of these children are helped by traditional means, others are not, or are even made worse by the existing repertoire of intervention. Accordingly, she challenges us—gently but with acuity—to rethink our traditions and to consider afresh how we intervene. The Thinking Heart is a book for today's analytically oriented clinician, dealing with today's patients, trying to find out what will work, but also trying to understand what works and why in the context of a vast literature.

We have the right author for the task.

The work of Jacques Lacan can be understood, in no small part, as a sustained challenge to the psychoanalytic establishment, which he saw as destroying Freud's radical project. Remember that whereas Freud had said that the worst possible training for a psychoanalyst would be medical school (Freud, 1926/1950b), the American group decided that only physicians could become analysts. This absurd reversal persisted until the well-known 1986 case of Welch v. American Psychoanalytic Association.

Remember also that Freud worked courageously to depathologize homosexuality, insisting that we are born with a bisexual disposition. The Oedipus complex of each individual has two sides—same-sex and cross-sex. Unfortunately, the same-sex story—according to which each little boy desires his father and sees his mother as a rival—has been erased from much psychoanalytic training and practice.

This bowdlerization of psychoanalysis outraged Lacan. He worried, presciently, that the ego psychologists wanted above all to help people adjust better to social norms, and that the vigorous pursuit of the truth of the unconscious—including the analysis of dreams—would be lost. I say “presciently” because I've noticed that many patients and supervisees who have already had long analyses come for treatment asking: “Do you think dreams are important? My analyst didn't seem interested.” Jeanne Wolf Bernstein (1999) has suggested that dream work has been set aside in favor of an overvaluation of countertransference as our new “royal road to the unconscious.”

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, Lacan worked under the rubric of “the return to Freud.” (He is known often to have said, in effect: It's up to you to be Lacanian; personally, I'm a Freudian.)

Dissociative processes, multiple self-states, trauma of nonrecognition, joint creative exploration, embodied communication

This article discusses several of Philip Bromberg's ideas that have resonated most powerfully for me: the therapist's feelings around his possible role as an agent of the patient's pain; the process of shifting among multiple self-states while remaining the same, applying for both participants; the situating of the self in a relational context, developmentally and in therapy; the core and pervasive impact of the chronic “trauma of nonrecognition,” and the patient's need to be needed as who he is, as a source of pleasure to another person. Building on Philip's characterization of “the analyst's ‘stumbling along and hanging in,’” the article introduces an expansion of my concept of the referential process to the relational context, as a process of joint creative exploration, including activation of experience, sharing of reveries, and joint reflection; and places this process in the context of current scientific work on embodied cognition and embodied communication.
